issues.legal_issue: A purported grant of state property that was not accepted before the former state transferred its administration did not prevent the property from vesting in the successor state.
material_facts: The ruler's letter described the state property as being given to one brother to use as a farm and to divide equally, but did not clearly identify the person with whom it was to be divided.
The ruler testified that the letter bore no official seal, that no official body or revenue authority had been directed to implement it, and that the property was not listed as his private property.
The purported recipient testified that he accepted the grant only after returning to India in November 1948.
The property was still state property when the former state transferred its administration under the covenant that formed the successor union.
issues.conclusion: Even assuming that the letter purported to grant the property, the grant was not accepted before the property vested in the successor union; the property therefore became state property of that union.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the covenant's provisions that vested the covenanting states' assets in the union while preserving each ruler's ownership only of private property, distinct from state property. It relied on the recipient's evidence that acceptance occurred only after the transfer of administration and on the ruler's evidence concerning the property's state character and the absence of official implementation.

predicates.purported_grant_of_state_property: A ruler purported to grant property that belonged to the ruler's state.
predicates.recipient_accepted_only_after_transfer: The proposed recipient accepted the purported grant only after the former state transferred its administration.
predicates.state_property_transferred_to_successor: The former state transferred its administration and state assets to a successor state.

issues.definition: When a ruler purports to grant state property, the recipient accepts only after the transfer, and the property is transferred as state property, the property vests in the successor state.

issues.legal_issue: An ordinary civil court cannot adjudicate a private claim to recover property from a successor state when the claim arises from a pre-constitutional covenant between rulers that involved the Government of India and continued in operation.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sued in ordinary civil courts to recover possession of property from the successor state.
Their claimed right to possession depended on whether the property passed to the successor state under the covenant forming the union.
The covenant was entered into by rulers of princely states before the Constitution and was concurred in by the Government of India, which guaranteed its provisions.
The covenant continued to operate after the Constitution came into force.
issues.conclusion: The suits were barred: the covenant was an act of state, and the courts lacked jurisdiction under Article 363(1) of the Constitution to decide the dispute arising from it. The appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on Article 363(1) of the Constitution, which bars courts from exercising jurisdiction over specified disputes arising from pre-constitutional treaties, agreements, or covenants entered into by rulers of Indian states with the Government of India or its predecessor and continued in operation after the Constitution. It also applied the act-of-state principle stated by the Constitution Bench in Dalmia Dadri Cement Ltd. v. Union of India, AIR 1958 SC 816: claims based on rights said to arise from a transfer of sovereignty under such an instrument cannot be enforced in court.

predicates.ordinary_civil_recovery_suit: A claimant brought an ordinary civil suit seeking possession of property from a successor state.
predicates.claim_arises_from_preconstitutional_stat: The claimant's asserted right to possession depends on a covenant made before the Constitution between rulers of states.
predicates.covenant_involved_government_and_remaine: The covenant involved the Government of India or its predecessor and continued in operation after the Constitution came into force.

issues.definition: When an ordinary civil recovery suit depends on a pre-constitutional state covenant involving the government that remained operational, the civil court lacks jurisdiction to decide the claim.
